summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for Frame Relay data terminal equipment, the devices at the edge of a Frame Relay connection. It was replaced by RFC 2115.

eli5.summary: A set of gauges for the equipment at the end of a Frame Relay line, so network helpers can check how it is doing.

questions: how to monitor frame relay dte
subtitle: SNMP management objects for Frame Relay data terminal equipment.

tldr.problem: Network administrators managing Frame Relay services needed a standard way to monitor and configure the equipment at the edge of Frame Relay connections across different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1315 defines SNMP managed objects organized into three groups: Data Link Connection Management Interface (DLCMI) configuration, virtual circuit state and statistics, and error tracking.
tldr.outcome: This MIB provided essential Frame Relay management but was superseded by RFC 2115 as Frame Relay technology matured.

today: RFC 1315 is obsoleted by RFC 2115, which provides updated Frame Relay management definitions. Frame Relay itself has largely been replaced by Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and modern cloud services.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Frame Relay is a packet-switching protocol optimized for data communications over Wide Area Networks. It operates at the data-link layer and offers lower overhead than earlier protocols by eliminating error correction and retransmission at each hop. RFC 1315 defines SNMP managed objects for Frame Relay Data Terminal Equipment (DTEs)—the equipment at the edge of a Frame Relay network that users control.

The RFC treats Frame Relay as a single physical interface layered with multiple virtual circuits identified by Data Link Connection Identifiers (DLCIs). Each DLCI represents a logical connection to a remote destination, whether permanent (configured in advance) or dynamic (created on demand). This view simplifies network management by grouping virtual connections with their underlying physical connection.
sections.eli5: Frame Relay links are fast, lean highways for data. Each company plugs equipment (a DTE) into the Frame Relay network and creates virtual circuits (like numbered lanes) to reach distant offices. This RFC explains how to ask that equipment questions via SNMP.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Management Groups
sections.content:
The Frame Relay MIB has three main components. The DLCMI (Data Link Connection Management Interface) group manages the protocol used to communicate with the Frame Relay network about virtual circuit status. It includes configuration parameters such as the polling interval (how often to ask the network for status), error thresholds (how many missed responses trigger an alarm), and the maximum number of virtual circuits allowed.

The Circuit group contains a table of information about each active or inactive virtual circuit. For each DLCI, the table records the circuit state, counters for frames and octets sent and received, congestion notification counts (FECN and BECN fields), and quality-of-service parameters such as committed burst rate and throughput. The Error group tracks the last error seen on the interface, its type, the data received, and the time of occurrence.
sections.eli5: The MIB has three drawers: one for negotiating with the Frame Relay network (DLCMI), one for tracking each virtual circuit's traffic and status, and one for recording what went wrong.

sections.title: Virtual Circuit Management
sections.content:
Each virtual circuit is represented as a row in the circuit table, indexed by the interface number and the DLCI. The frCircuitState object can be set by the administrator to 'active', 'inactive', or 'invalid' to control the circuit's operational state. When a circuit is created or deleted by the network (via the Data Link Connection Management Interface), the DLCMI automatically updates the table; managers can also create or delete circuits manually via SNMP.

The circuit table includes counters for frames and octets sent and received on that circuit since its creation. Two fields record congestion notification bits (FECN and BECN) received from the network: FECN signals forward congestion (the path to the destination is congested), while BECN signals backward congestion (the path back is congested). These counters help administrators detect when the network is overloaded and may trigger traffic shaping or rerouting policies.
sections.eli5: Each virtual circuit has a status light (active, inactive, or off) and counters for traffic. Congestion bits tell whether the line ahead is busy or the line back is busy—like traffic signals on a highway.

sections.title: DLCI and Address Formats
sections.content:
A Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI) is a 10- to 13-bit number that uniquely identifies a virtual circuit on a Frame Relay interface. The RFC supports multiple address formats standardized by ITU-T: Q.921 (13-bit DLCI), Q.922 March 90 (11-bit), Q.922 November 90 (10-bit), and final Q.922. The address length (two, three, or four octets) is configurable per interface to match the network's standard. The RFC allows administrators to set the maximum supported DLCI value and the maximum number of concurrent virtual circuits, accommodating different service levels and network capabilities.

The DLCMI also tracks the Link Management Interface type in use. Common types include 'noLmiConfigured' (no automatic discovery), 'lmiRev1' (Cisco's proprietary extension), and ANSI T1.617 variants (standards-based management). The polling interval and error thresholds ensure that equipment can detect when the connection to the network has failed and halt traffic accordingly.
sections.eli5: Each virtual circuit gets a number (DLCI). Different Frame Relay standards use different-sized numbers. Managers set the maximum expected circuits and choose how often to check if the network is still reachable.

sections.title: Error Tracking and Traps
sections.content:
The Error group records problems encountered on the Frame Relay interface. The frErrType object identifies the last error, distinguishing between various failure modes: 'receiveShort' (frame too small), 'receiveLong' (frame exceeds maximum size), 'illegalDLCI' (unknown DLCI), 'dlcmiProtoErr' (protocol violation), and others. The frErrData field contains the offending packet or frame, and frErrTime records when the error occurred.

RFC 1315 defines one trap: frDLCIStatusChange, which fires when a virtual circuit transitions between active, inactive, or invalid states. Administrators can enable or disable this trap via the frTrapState object. This trap alerts management systems to circuit failures or recoveries so they can investigate or trigger failover procedures.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong—a frame is too big, a circuit drops—the equipment remembers what happened. It can also send a signal (a trap) to the manager when a circuit changes status.
